subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Fungal infections range from superficial skin disease to life‑threatening opportunistic infections in immunocompromised patients. Clinical reasoning focuses on history, simple bedside tests, and empiric therapy when advanced diagnostics are unavailable.

sections.p: Fungi are ubiquitous; disease severity depends on host immunity and organism virulence. In East Africa, common superficial infections (tinea, candidiasis) coexist with opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis, Aspergillus, Cryptococcus) in HIV and TB patients.
Fungi are eukaryotes with chitinous cell walls. They reproduce by spores (conidia, arthroconidia) and can form biofilms. Many are dimorphic, changing form with temperature.
b: Spore dissemination via air or contact

sections.p: Transmission is usually airborne (Aspergillus, Pneumocystis) or via skin contact (tinea). In low‑resource settings, environmental exposure (dust, decaying vegetation) and poor hygiene increase risk.
Superficial mycoses affect skin, hair, nails; systemic mycoses involve lungs, CNS, or bloodstream, often in HIV, TB, or malnutrition.
History of exposure, HIV status, and symptom chronology guide diagnosis. Bedside tests (KOH prep, Gram stain, India ink) are useful when labs are limited.
b: KOH prep of skin scrapings – detects hyphae

t.b: Shows hyphae or spores; positive indicates fungal infection
Detects cryptococcal capsule in CSF; positive suggests cryptococcal meningitis
Look for bilateral ground‑glass opacities in PCP or cavitating lesions in Aspergillus

sections.p: Treat the underlying immunosuppression first. Empiric antifungals are chosen based on likely pathogen and drug availability. Monitor for toxicity and drug interactions.
b: TMP‑SMX for PCP (if available) or clindamycin + primaquine in resource‑poor settings

t.b: Treats PCP; monitor renal function and CBC
Treats Candida; avoid in severe hepatic disease

sections.p: Remember that PCP does not respond to fluconazole. In HIV patients with cough and dyspnea, consider PCP before bacterial pneumonia. Use KOH prep when microscopy is available; if not, empiric TMP‑SMX is reasonable in suspected PCP.
Superficial fungal infections can mimic bacterial cellulitis; PCP can resemble bacterial pneumonia or TB. Distinguish by clinical course, response to antibiotics, and simple tests.
KOH prep may be negative if sample is inadequate; India ink may be negative early in cryptococcal meningitis. Chest X‑ray findings are non‑specific.
For suspected PCP with hypoxia, start oxygen and empiric TMP‑SMX immediately. For suspected invasive Aspergillus with haemoptysis, stabilize airway and consider amphotericin B if available.
Monitor for treatment response: resolution of fever, improved oxygenation, and repeat imaging if available. Watch for drug toxicity.
Urgent care needed for severe respiratory distress, haemoptysis, altered mental status, or signs of sepsis.

t.a: What is the first line treatment for PCP in a setting without TMP‑SMX?
t.b: Clindamycin plus primaquine is an alternative, but TMP‑SMX remains preferred if available.
Yes, especially in neutropenic patients; treat with fluconazole or echinocandins.

t.a: How to differentiate tinea from bacterial cellulitis?
t.b: Tinea shows ring‑like scaling and KOH positivity; cellulitis shows warmth, erythema, and responds to antibiotics.

faq.q: What is the most common fungal infection in HIV patients in East Africa?
faq.a: Pneumocystis pneumonia is common, especially with CD4 <200.

faq.q: Which test is useful when a lab is unavailable?
faq.a: KOH prep of skin scrapings or simple Gram stain of sputum can guide empiric therapy.

faq.q: Why does PCP not respond to fluconazole?
faq.a: Pneumocystis lacks ergosterol, so fluconazole is ineffective.

exam: A 32‑year‑old HIV patient presents with dry cough and progressive dyspnea. What is the first empiric treatment? — Start TMP‑SMX immediately; consider oxygen if hypoxic.

A 45‑year‑old TB patient develops fever and weight loss. Chest X‑ray shows a cavitating lesion. What is the differential? — Aspergillus, TB relapse, bacterial abscess; obtain sputum culture and consider empiric antifungal if high suspicion.

A 28‑year‑old woman with chronic cough has a normal chest X‑ray but hypoxia. What bedside test can help? — Perform a simple KOH prep of sputum for fungal elements; if negative, consider PCP and start TMP‑SMX.

A patient with suspected fungal meningitis has a negative India ink stain. What next? — Repeat CSF collection and consider cryptococcal antigen test; if unavailable, start empiric fluconazole if Candida is likely.
A child with tinea capitis shows scaling and hair loss. Why is KOH prep important? — It confirms fungal hyphae, distinguishing from bacterial folliculitis.
A patient on amphotericin B develops fever and chills. What is the likely cause? — Infusion‑related reaction; pre‑medicate with antihistamine and reduce infusion rate.
